title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
dek: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
why: Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; the value is in the concrete scenes and in how a single play grew. Anyone looking for methodology or industry judgment can skip it.
who: People in charity work, theatre and community workshops; content people who want to understand why inclusion can't rest on goodwill alone; practitioners and volunteers in disability issues.
skip: The rehearsal clip at the start and the submission call-out at the end can be skipped.

points.h: Disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm
points.body: Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Han Ya (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of them, a woman in her thirties, had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at New Year, it felt to her "like walking a little dog or cat." Later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. Once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another woman, a visually impaired mother, was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, on the grounds that "you can't see, you can't raise a child"; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These accounts made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

points.h: Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
points.body: A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair, and when she moved house the only people she could ask for help were friends who also use wheelchairs, hauling load after load with bags hanging all over their chairs. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright — they'd have finished in half a day. The colleague paused, then said, I don't know any able-bodied people. She had not a single able-bodied friend; even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even get the chance to meet, "you have no chance at inclusion at all." That was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre.

points.h: Writing able-bodied people as the discriminated original sinners
points.body: The troupe Leyi's first play, Ni Zhuan Wei Lai (逆转未来), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification — electronic eyes, cochlear implants and the like; the remaining few able-bodied people are branded original sinners for "the crime of starting the nuclear war" and pushed to the margins of society. Yaoyao's logic was that since she herself is a person with situs inversus, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights the able-bodied have to fight for — what she calls writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The plot's core: an original-sinner father, to spare his son the suffering of an able-bodied body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to cut off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of his own blood; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about original sinners and augmented humans.

points.h: How the unseen and the unheard partner up
points.body: Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled into a pairing by deaf actor Li Ning at an audition, and his first reaction was blank: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to trace on the back of his hand, tapping once when it was his line. Director Ma Yan says blind and deaf performers sharing a stage already exists abroad: the deaf performer's hand rests on the visually impaired performer's hand, so the latter can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says he had grown up around deaf people, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with a communication barrier, "absolutely impossible to communicate" — a barrier that was almost insurmountable. After this collaboration he and Li Ning became close friends. The troupe also had to solve sign-language interpretation, live-caption screens, and a volunteer for every visually impaired actor to provide audio description.

points.h: Visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones
points.body: Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact "cheating": they wore earphones, listened to the lines at several times normal speed, and delivered them fluently on stage, so the director had no way to assess them and could only marvel at how fast the visually impaired actors got their lines down. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language, so he could only watch everyone signing and grin along, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks came out.

points.h: She received the best production award from the ICU
points.body: In 2024 Ni Zhuan Wei Lai was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao's heart gave out and she was admitted to the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and their members dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more food, thinking "how could it possibly be us." In the end they won Best Production, the festival's highest award, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood and led the applause. The news reached the ICU at the same moment as the award, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. That October the play was invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival as the first integrated disability production, the only piece in the "Nothing Is Impossible" section.

points.h: After writing this play, she changed her answer and chose not to be born
points.body: The second play, Wo Xuan Ze Chu Sheng (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health and family circumstances, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families, there are deaf parents who must honestly tell their child you'll be deaf too, a husband who deceives his wife into having a child, a family that favours boys over girls, and a final story adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script, because their life experiences were eerily similar — only the conditions differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had it to do over, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced into this world with no choice.

points.h: Cai Cong and she give opposite answers to the same question
points.body: The episode sets the deaf couple in Wo Xuan Ze Chu Sheng against the real-life Cai Cong: Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume that such a life was not worth starting merely because the child might also be visually impaired; they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument over this choice persists. The question the episode poses: when a family makes a choice, how much choice do they actually have?

quotes.text: She was taken aback too, and said, I don't know any able-bodied people. She didn't have a single able-bodied friend — even she and her friends all used wheelchairs.
I said I'm a person with situs inversus, so we might as well flip the whole society too and see what happens.
This play makes you think. The sincerity of the performances covers the flaws in technique. And most striking of all is the troupe's refusal to be pitied.
None of us could get through it, because we felt our life experiences were eerily similar — only the conditions were different, but the experiences were the same.
I actually used to say I would choose to be born too, but if it were now, I might choose not to be born.
But perhaps what's really worth asking is: when a family makes a choice, how much choice do they actually have?
He was like a blade of grass in the wind, about to wither — but he was always growing.
